task: Execute the reverse-engineering drill on Palladium Fantasy 1e combat, character progression, and subsystem integration.
delivery: current canonical drill plus guided analysis
observations: Active defense creates meaningful defensive agency but adds a resolution step to applicable incoming attacks, so its execution cost scales with attack count and participant count.
The rules use several unrelated resolution families across combat, skills, attributes, saves, recovery, and other subsystems; learning one procedure does not reliably teach the next.
A missing formal rule can be deliberate delegation to player or referee judgment rather than an accidental mechanical hole.
notes: The drill produced architectural observations without reducing the analysis to a preference judgment.

task: Compare Rifts Ultimate Edition against its older Palladium chassis using the reverse-engineering drill and inspect how later mechanics integrate with inherited rules.
delivery: current canonical drill plus guided comparison
observations: Adding new domains without refactoring the core produced conversion rules, stacking exceptions, parallel damage scales, and situational patches that increased completeness faster than coherence.
A rule can remain executable while accumulating adapter logic that signals architectural mismatch between subsystems.
Legacy preservation can make the game serve an inherited mechanic rather than reevaluating whether that mechanic still expresses the expanded design requirements.
notes: The same analysis vocabulary used on Palladium Fantasy transferred to a later edition and exposed accretion rather than merely greater rule volume.

task: Compare Star Frontiers and FrontierSpace as examples of detailed science-fiction RPG design, focusing on reusable primitives, action economy, adjudication, and subsystem reuse.
delivery: current canonical drill plus cross-system comparison
observations: Detailed rules remained easier to reason about when many situations reused the same probability grammar or action-check operation instead of introducing new resolution families.
FrontierSpace's multi-action penalty concentrates several tactical tradeoffs into one reusable rule, so added complexity directly creates decisions about present action versus later defense.
Explicitly allowing adjudication through existing abilities and skills limits rule growth when an edge case can already be expressed by the system's mechanical vocabulary.
Mechanical detail was allocated according to play importance, as shown by simplified minor NPCs and scalable detail rather than fully specifying every entity.
notes: The drill transferred from critique of failure modes to recognition of healthy crunch and constructive architecture.

task: Compare Knight Hawks starship construction with FrontierSpace vehicle and starship design to test whether extensive configuration creates meaningful build differentiation.
delivery: current canonical drill plus construction-system stress test
observations: Knight Hawks offers substantial construction procedure while hull-size dependencies cause many same-class ships to converge on similar mechanical identities.
A construction system can expose many configuration choices while still having a narrow practical possibility space when parent variables pre-determine most downstream behavior.
Separating size from independently adjustable performance and capability parameters increases conceptual breadth without requiring every concept to ignore balance constraints.
notes: The comparison produced a repeatable stress test: attempt several different intended roles within one broad class and check whether the rules pull them toward the same final build.
